newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: INTERVIEW-Sasol hunts for black partner i.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Sasol hunts for black partner i.

text.p: South Africa's Sasol Ltd, one of the apartheid era's most effective sanctions busters, is hunting for a black empowerment partner in its chemicals operations, new managing director Pieter Cox said on Wednesday.

The fuels firm, whose coal-to-oil technology allowed white-ruled South Africa to produce its own fuel during the years of economic isolation, has already signed a black empowerment deal with Naledi Petroleum Industries.
That deal will create a multi-million rand black-controlled oil company in which Sasol will hold a 22.5 percent stake.
Cox told Reuters in an interview that Sasol was now exploring similar deals for its downstream chemicals businesses.
"We can see (a deal with) a group similar to Naledi that has an interest in one or other of the downstream chemicals sectors," Cox said.
The Naledi venture is to be launched on June 1 and will establish 40 service stations pumping more than an average of 275,000 litres of fuel a month over the next three years.

Sasol has stated that it is considering entering the retail fuel market. Cox said the Naledi venture would not satisfy Sasol's ambitions in this direction, but he declined to confirm that Sasol was poised to launch a retail operation.

"We are keeping our options open and if we believe it is in our interests that we should enter the retail arena in order to realise our ambitions and growth then we will do so... but there is no absolute need to be in the retail market," he said.

Sasol has always been a source of controversy in the energy industry due to government protection against violent falls in the oil price. The government's current price floor where subsidies would be triggered is $18 a barrel, but that will fall to $17 by July as part of a process of gradually phasing it out.
Cox said Sasol had received no subsidy since November and was prepared to compete on a level playing field.
Cox, who replaced Paul Kruger at the start of the year, said Sasol had a three-pronged strategy for growth.
The firm aims to develop more technology that will add value to its fuel stream and also to boost capacity at existing plants by removing bottlenecks.
The third part of the strategy is to hunt for partners for offshore ventures with its Fischer Tropsch conversion technology -- a way of breaking down gas into useful or valuable petrochemicals.
"Promising opportunities are being investigated and in the foreseeable future we will be able to make public the first of those ventures," Cox said.
Cox added that the first of several possible deals could be unveiled within two years, but the agreements will not involve licensing out the cutting edge technology.
"At this stage we don't foresee licensing our technology. It will be with a Sasol equity holding. We are looking for and talking to potentially suitable partners," he said.
The drive for partnerships is part of Sasol's expansion plans into the rest of Africa.

Due to South Africa's new political climate Cox said Sasol now finds that its name carries weight in a continent where it was once better known as a favourite target for African National Congress (ANC) bomb attacks.
"We are of Africa and we understand Africa. Particularly under the new dispensation (in South Africa) there is a political affinity for us," he said.
Sasol has created an exploration and production business, Sasol Petroleum International, which is pursuing opportunities in Algeria, Angola, Congo, Namibia and Mozambique.
